title: The Quiet Truth of Oakhaven Academy
markdown:
The rehearsal room at Oakhaven Academy was a cauldron of frayed nerves and fevered dreams, and Clara the ebony cat sat at the grand piano as if the keys were the only honest furniture in the building. Her paws coaxed melody in a cadence that whispered rather than shouted. She knew the exact strength of the stage lights, the wheeze of the sound system, and the delicate balance of student actors still growing into their voices. That knowledge was not a speech. It was the room as it actually was.

Jules the raven, stage manager, presided from a catwalk, feathers like polished obsidian, architect of invisible transitions and tamer of theatrical temperament. His voice could cut the din with a precise “Places, everyone!”

The room, however, yearned for glorious falsehoods: opulence, echo, a budget it did not have. Bartholomew Buttercup, prop master, had decreed that the centrepiece would be a magnificent solid-gold candelabra, rumoured to have been liberated from a forgotten royal treasury.

“It’s the ambiance!” he declared, mustache quivering with invention. “It screams legacy! It whispers masterpiece!”

Clara watched him fuss over the ridiculously heavy thing, which she suspected was spray-painted papier-mâché, and let out a tiny sigh. In a dusty corner sat the real candelabra: carefully polished brass that would actually give a warm glow. That one would do the job. The ostentatious lie was precarious.

Jules, high above, had seen this hunger for the spectacular before: students’ eyes widening, Bartholomew’s claims swelling. “More velvet!” Bartholomew boomed at the backdrop. “And the trumpets — harbingers of dawn!” He ignored the wheezy sounds the student trumpeters were producing.

Clara played a delicate interlude that sounded like practicalities. Thick velvet would swallow the lights. The sound system would not carry brass above a fabricated gold glare. The performance would be best with what they had.

The director swept in on a rustle of expensive silk. “My dears! The Mayor and the critics arrive in twenty minutes! Everything must be perfect!” Her gaze landed on the golden candelabra. Horror dawned.

“That thing,” she shrieked, trembling finger aloft, “is gaudy. A mockery. An insult to art!”

Bartholomew sputtered. The room panicked: more light, extra silk, the candelabra too heavy to move if it fell.

Jules swooped from the catwalk and landed on the edge of Clara’s piano. He looked from director to Buttercup to Clara, paws poised above the keys.

“This,” he said, in a surprisingly deep baritone, “is an excellent idea, which is precisely why I distrust it.” A wing indicated the neglected brass. “That will let the actors be seen. Warmth, not glare. It does not threaten to topple the theatrical universe.”

Silence. Eyes found the unassuming brass, then Clara. A small nod passed between cat and raven.

“But the gold,” Bartholomew stammered.

Jules did not lecture. He hopped once, toward the corner. Clara rose, and together they lifted the brass candelabra into the light. It was heavier than rumour and lighter than lie. Clara polished it until it gleamed, then set it, with something like reverence, centre stage. The papier-mâché masterpiece went back to the dust.

When the curtain rose, the brass cast a gentle inviting glow. Students, no longer competing with a falsehood, found their voices. Dances could be seen. Clara’s accompaniment wove through without shouting. High above, Jules watched. Beside the piano, Clara let out a deep, contented purr. The evening, bathed in honest light, simply worked.
characters: Clara (cat rehearsal pianist), Jules (raven stage manager), Bartholomew (papier-mache prop master)
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
author: StoryGen Community
